name: Duvos
tagline: An AI assistant product sold at duvo.ai, with a public footprint thin enough that its exact scope is hard to pin down.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Honest disclosure first: we know very little about this one, and the entry is written accordingly. Products in this shape, an AI assistant sold on a short .ai domain, are usually a hosted model plus a prompt layer, a few connectors, and a clean dashboard, and that pattern is genuinely a one-session build for an agent. The parts that do not replicate in a session are the connectors: every integration is its own OAuth app, its own review process, its own rate limits. If Duvos turns out to be trained on something proprietary or shipping its own model weights, downgrade this to a no, and if it turns out to be a chat box with memory, upgrade it to a yes. Until the scope is verified, treat the DIY version as a working personal substitute with worse plumbing.
coreLoopDIY: A local assistant that chats against a hosted model, remembers prior conversations, and can run a small set of tools you define yourself.
requirements: An API key for a hosted model provider, billed per token
A machine or cheap VPS to keep it running if you want it reachable from your phone
whatYouLose: Prebuilt connectors to your calendar, mail and docs, each of which is a separate OAuth slog
Whatever prompt and evaluation tuning the vendor did that you cannot see
A mobile app and push notifications
Someone else absorbing model cost spikes and provider outages
Any proprietary data or model the product may actually be built on, which is the part this entry cannot confirm
moatNotes: Thin public information means the moat assessment here is provisional, not researched.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the assistant category lives or dies on connectors and polish, not on the model, and nobody wants to maintain six OAuth apps to ask a question about their own calendar. Paying also means the prompt tuning, retry logic and context handling are someone else's problem, and those are the parts that quietly eat a weekend and then keep eating evenings. A personal build is fine when you are the only user and you are happy to fix it yourself.
notes: Entry written with thin information on the product itself; the build prompt targets the generic shape, not verified feature parity.
prompt:
Build a personal AI assistant I run myself. Single user, local first, no accounts.

Stack, non negotiable: TypeScript, Node 20, Fastify for the HTTP layer, SQLite via better-sqlite3 for storage, and a plain server rendered UI using Fastify static files plus htmx. No Next.js, no React, no ORM, no auth provider.

What to build:
1. A chat UI at / with a message list, a text input, and streaming responses rendered as they arrive.
2. A model client that talks to one hosted provider, read the base URL, model name and API key from .env. Support streaming. Handle 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff and surface a readable error in the UI instead of a blank bubble.
3. Conversations stored in SQLite: tables for conversation, message, and tool_call. Sidebar lists conversations, clicking one loads it, you can rename and delete.
4. Persistent memory: a notes table the assistant can write to and read from via tools, injected into the system prompt as a short bulleted block, capped at 2000 characters so it cannot blow up context.
5. Tool calling with exactly three tools to start: read_file and write_file scoped to a ./workspace directory with path traversal blocked, and web_fetch that pulls a URL and strips it to text. Log every tool call to the DB and show it collapsed in the transcript.
6. A /settings page to edit the system prompt, the model name and the temperature, stored in SQLite, no restart required.

Explicitly out of scope: calendar, email and Slack integrations, OAuth of any kind, multi user support, billing, telemetry, analytics, and a mobile app. Do not add them, do not stub them.

Secrets live in .env, ship a .env.example. Include a README with setup in under ten lines and a single npm run dev that works from a clean clone. Add a token counter per conversation so I can see what this is costing me. Keep the whole thing under roughly 1500 lines and do not install a dependency you do not use.
